title: Can Nepal’s hydropower boom withstand a changing Himalaya? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Can Nepal’s hydropower boom withstand a changing Himalaya?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
On the morning of August 26, Bal Bahadur Majhi, 50, was clearing firewood, rocks, and sand from the tunnel at the Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Project in Timure. The plant diverts part of the river into the tunnel and uses its steep drop to generate electricity.



Then he heard what he described as explosions in the distance. Before he could make sense of them, a landslide barrelled into the tunnel, and a slurry of mud, rocks, and water tossed him and pulled him under. When the water finally dropped to his neck, the tunnel was pitch dark and blocked.



“We never realised how dangerous it was,” he said. “They had told us to go in a particular direction if there was a flood; there had been a small one last year, but we never imagined something as disastrous could happen.”

For two days and two nights, Majhi stayed inside the tunnel with his co-workers, without water or food. They palmed their way through the darkness for an exit, but the flood had destroyed the walls, pillars, and water pipes. “We heard helicopters outside, and it gave us hope that someone would come,” he said.

Majhi does not recall how he and three others finally got out. His rescue by the Nepali Army remains a blur.



Hydropower has long been touted as Nepal’s “white gold” — a source of wealth and a pillar of the country’s ambitions for economic transformation. But as the country aims to generate 30,000 MW by 2035, increasingly destructive disasters are exposing the risks of that pursuit. The question now reaches far beyond one power plant: can Nepal turn its rivers into an engine of growth without putting workers, communities and its fragile Himalayan environment at greater risk?



Rasuwagadhi has become a stark example of Nepal’s cascading and compounding disasters. Three floods hit the plant in 15 months. The first was a glacier lake outburst flood (GLOF) in July 2025 , then a sediment-laden flood in July 2026 . In August 2026, a rock-ice avalanche on Langtang Lirung triggered another flood. The disaster killed or left more than 6,700 people missing and damaged 12 operating hydropower projects, 15 under-construction projects, and transmission lines. Losses are estimated at Rs150 billion , more than 90 percent of Nepal Electricity Authority’s revenue last fiscal year.

Despite warnings, Nepal has continued to put more plants and people along its rivers. Some energy experts consider the Rasuwa disaster a once-in-a-century event that should not derail Nepal’s plans. Others question whether Nepal’s pursuit of economic growth has kept pace with more volatile disasters, a changing climate, geopolitics and the needs of its own citizens.



“We need to revisit our goals,” said water expert Ajaya Dixit, who has authored several books including ‘Nepalma Bipad’ (Disasters in Nepal). “Maybe they are fine, but after the Rasuwa disaster, we need to pause and reflect. We can’t continue business as usual.”

Dixit says Nepal has designed its hydropower in silos, and that over the last 50 years, human intervention has changed the landscapes.

“Rivers are not what they used to be 100 years ago—we have diverted them, we have dammed them,” he said. “The processes within the hydrological cycle have changed. But our institutions, our knowledge base, our understanding, have remained rooted in an older imagination. ”

Rush for ‘white gold’

Nepal’s hydropower boom took off in the last decade. Earlier, when there were fewer plants, the state-owned NEA owned most of them. As projects grew, Nepal developed its own pool of hydropower engineers, builders and designers.

Severe power cuts — with loadshedding lasting up to 18 hours a day at its peak — and the pursuit of prosperity drove more investment. State-sponsored campaigns such as “ Nepal’s waters, [the] people’s investments ” ( Nepal ko pani, janatako lagani ) urged citizens to buy hydropower shares rather than depend on foreign powers.

But the appeal went beyond nationalism. Hydropower was profitable. Selling shares allowed investors to recover their money without having their capital tied up in a plant for years, while power purchase agreements with the NEA offered a predictable market for the electricity generated, at contractually agreed rates.



“People were literally flying in helicopters, looking for bends in rivers,” said energy expert Satish Joshi. “The economics of hydro is essentially about catching the elevation difference — the shorter the distance over which that drop occurs, the better the site.”

Hydropower licensing has risen sharply in recent years, with the number of licenses issued annually more than tripling from 79 in 2024 to 241 in 2026 .

“The private sector poured its life savings into Nepal’s hydropower,” said Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice president of the Independent Power Producers Association Nepal. “Today, the private sector generates more than 80 percent of Nepal’s electricity. Counting plants under development, that will soon be more than 90 percent.”

At what cost?

Hydropower accounts for only two percent of Nepal’s GDP. But given its potential, Nepal’s leaders see it as a “ vital cross-border asset ”. Writing in the NEA’s annual report before the Rasuwa floods in August, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said: “We must act like the giant, multi-billion-dollar corporate enterprise that we are.” He urged the NEA family to “regard these milestones (exporting 2,794 GWh of energy) “not as the culmination of our journey, but as the foundation for an even more ambitious future.”

For now, the targets remain intact, said Mohan Kumar Shakya, joint secretary at the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources, and Irrigation. “We have formed a scientific committee to determine why the disaster happened and whether it will happen again. Its technical and policy recommendations will determine whether we need to modify the target,” he said.

For Dixit, however, the Rasuwa disaster exposed major gaps between policy and practice.

“Rivers have water, energy, biodiversity, and sediments. But modern water development focuses only on water and energy. This is the development model we inherited, that harnesses flowing water for energy at the cost of biodiversity,” he said.

Nepal now has 197 hydropower projects in operation, and an additional 260 plants under construction, and 241 with licenses for survey.

“This kind of disaster is the first of many to come. The government has handed out hydropower licenses so haphazardly that there is hardly any river untouched,” said hydroengineer Anugya Sapkota. “Sometimes the licences even overlap on the same stretch of the river.”

The NEA’s multiple roles limit independent oversight. It is the country’s principal electricity buyer, generator, transmitter and distributor, leaving few institutional checks on its decisions.

The tunnel entrance of the 22-megawatt Chilime Hydropower Plant in Syafrubesi, Rasuwa, damaged by the Bhotekoshi floods. Power generation at the plant has been halted after floodwater and mud inundated the project. RSS

“Because governance is weak, any monitoring becomes an opportunity for rent-seeking. The lack of a truly independent agency in Nepal compounds this problem,” said Joshi.



All 11 experts interviewed for this story described the government’s environmental assessments as inadequate — some called them “a sham.” Human rights organisations have also documented violations of Indigenous communities’ rights and environmental safeguards, including in projects financed by the Asian Development Bank, the European Investment Bank, and the World Bank.



An investigation in Kantipur from August also shows developers forging Indigenous people’s signatures for free, prior and informed consent, destroying habitats of endangered species such as red pandas and golden masheer , and encroaching on up to 90 times more land than agreed. In some communities, developers blasted hills to build tunnels without adequate consultations, triggering major landslides.



“The developers are so stingy they don’t even release the mandatory 10 percent water flow and try to sell every last drop,” said Sapkota. Minimum flow requirements are intended to protect aquatic life and riverbeds, while limiting harm to downstream settlements.

Lama acknowledged the problem. He said the 2015 earthquake had dried up some water sources, but electricity-generation targets in the contracts were never revised. Developers were therefore caught between declining water supplies and contractual expectations, even as local communities and environmentalists pressed hydropower operators to release more water. Lama cautioned that changing these practices would take time.

“Companies are indeed not releasing even the minimum flow required,” he said.

If all planned projects go ahead, experts warn, Nepal could end up “piping” all its rivers.



According to Sapkota, the only stretches of Nepal’s rivers that are free of hydropower are inside national parks. “They must release 50 percent of the water in the rivers, and it isn’t profitable for the developers,” she said.



Who really benefits?

Hydropower has helped expand electricity access. More than 97 percent of households are now connected to the electricity grid, compared with 62 percent a decade ago. But a connection does not mean people can reliably use the electricity their country generates.

“Nepal has robbed its people of the benefits of hydropower,” said Bishal Thapa, who has worked in the energy sector for nearly three decades. “The [transmission] lines are so weak that every time there is a storm, they go down. If five pumps are switched on, the system stops working. People cannot even run motors for agriculture; they need three-phase lines, but there isn’t enough voltage to operate them.”

According to Thapa, the transmission lines will stretch for 60-70 kilometers in remote villages, when they should extend only 20 to 30 kilometers. “By the time the line reaches the last house in the village, there isn’t enough voltage to run even a simple fan,” he said.



Shakya said the NEA was working to improve the grid. But energy experts argue that the benefits of hydropower must also be measured in the royalties and jobs communities receive.

Under Nepal’s constitution, revenue from natural resources, including hydropower, is shared among three tiers of government: 50 percent to the federal government and 25 percent each to the provincial and local governments.



Karnali remains one of Nepal’s last free-flowing rivers , sustaining settlements and fisheries, and replenishing aquifers. But keeping it free-flowing raises a difficult question: how can communities benefit economically if hydropower is restricted?

“Try telling the people of the Karnali region that they won’t get any royalty because we want to keep Karnali free-flowing,” said Joshi, who argued that communities should not be deprived of economic benefits as a result.

Sanjib Oli, chair of Bigu Rural Municipality in Dolakha, home to Nepal’s largest operational hydropower plant, Upper Tamakoshi, questioned whether royalties had made a real difference.

The flood-damaged tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, from where two persons were rescued alive, in Rasuwa. A joint teamof the Nepali Army and Chinese rescuers was deployed for search and rescue in the tunnel. Hemanta Shrestha/TKP

“We get a meager royalty, and even that never comes on time,” he said. “There have been no new schools in the area since the plant was built. There is no paved road. They hire skilled labor from elsewhere, and even the vegetables they eat are imported.”

For many Nepalis, however, hydropower projects remain an important source of income, particularly during construction.

Raju BK, 28, whose cousin Bikram BK, 27, remains missing after the floods at the Upper Trishuli project, said the job had been the first regular wage anyone in their family had earned.



“We are Kami Dalits. We make sickle and spade, and in return people give us seasonal crops like corn,” he said.

Bikram earned Rs 16,000 a month, plus Rs 50 an hour for tunnel work, bringing his monthly income to about Rs 25,000 — about 26 percent above Nepal’s per capita monthly income. “It was hardly enough to support his two young children,” said Raju. “Unlike other people, we don’t own land and cannot farm to get by.”

Raju and other Dalit families in Pangsang are now worried about their future after the destruction of the hydropower plants.

What’s next?

The cycle of development, destruction, and rebuilding has put Nepal in a quandary, especially when it comes to hydropower.

Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says the choice is not between a lot of hydropower or none. “We need a nuanced position that recognizes the value of human life, learns from the past and minimizes future harm,” he said.

He called for an independent panel of experts to investigate what happened, identify what went wrong, and ensure that lessons are implemented. “Project developers and financiers must be held accountable for making hydropower projects safer,” he said.



Even if the Rasuwa disaster was an exceptional, extreme event, that does not explain why workers had no escape route, said Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a senior climate change specialist.

“A tunnel could collapse on its own. An earthquake could block it. It doesn’t have to be debris from a flood,” he said. “Where was the escape route in those cases? The fact that there wasn’t one is a huge gap. If we dismiss this as a once-in-a-century event, we will suffer again. It will happen again.”

Although underground power plants suffered less structural damage than those above ground, their tunnels became death traps for hundreds of workers.

“Why were hundreds of people working in the tunnels without a proper evacuation system? The hydropower companies will get their insurance and leave, but why weren’t the workers insured the same way as the infrastructure?” asked Thapa.

Experts also suggested halting construction during the monsoon, when the risk of floods and landslides is highest.

The failure to release even the mandatory 10 percent flow “points not only to poor compliance but to deeper problems of a regulatory system with no teeth to enforce and monitor its own rules,” said Thakkar. “If a project is required to have a functioning early warning system and it doesn’t, but no one checks and there are no consequences, of course there will be downstream disasters.”

The Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Project. Photo courtesy of Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Project

Experts also want changes to how hydropower is governed. They recommended giving local governments a greater oversight role, separating the NEA’s conflicting roles as generator, buyer and seller, and expanding regulation beyond the Department of Electricity Development’s narrow mandate. The Water and Energy Commission Secretariat, they argue, is better placed to assess hydropower alongside its effects on communities and the environment.



Sapkota said the government could limit the number of plants on each river by controlling power purchase agreements, even though many licenses have already been issued. She also suggested moving plants farther downstream. This would not necessarily undermine the targets, she said, but could give communities more time to respond to floods.



Experts like Sapkota, Joshi and Kandel also called for basin-wide studies to determine how much hydropower each river basin can sustain. Rather than many small run-of-river projects, they suggested fewer, larger storage reservoirs that could regulate flows.

But Dixit cautioned that changing the location or type of plant alone would not protect infrastructure from a disaster on the scale of Rasuwa. The underlying problem, experts say, is that hydropower development has not adequately accounted for the distinctive conditions of Himalayan rivers.



“Nepal largely adopted hydropower technologies and design approaches developed elsewhere. But Himalayan rivers are very different — they carry enormous sediment loads,” said Shrestha, the climate change specialist. “Yet there is very limited research on how designs should be adapted to Nepal’s conditions.”



Climate change makes that adaptation more urgent. Although developers account for floods and earthquakes in their designs, GLOFs, landslides, and rock-ice avalanche floods are difficult to predict.

“Climate change is altering rainfall, snowfall, and glacier melt, bringing both excess water and drought,” said Shrestha. “More intense rainfall can also accelerate erosion, increasing the sediment carried by rivers and damaging hydropower infrastructure.”

Yet projects often ignore these changes or treat climate assessments as a box-ticking exercise. Projects being designed today must anticipate how conditions could change over the next 10 to 20 years and adapt, Shrestha said.

The challenge is paying for resilience. Private investors are wary of the extra costs of building plants to withstand extreme events. “Ultimately the cost of designing hydropower projects to withstand once-in-a-thousand year disasters such as Rasuwa would fall on ordinary people,” said Lama.

Others argue that investing upfront in resilience saves money in the long run. “For every dollar invested in strengthening a hydropower plant, four dollars in damage can be avoided,” said Shrestha.



Bibek Kandel, an energy expert and adviser to the energy minister, suggested that the country seek climate-justice funding to cover some of the costs, though he was skeptical it would come through. “Getting climate justice for Nepal will not be easy. But ask for it, and put your weight behind what you will do with that money,” he said.



The costs and risks of more resilient hydropower plants have also raised questions about Nepal’s 30,000 MW target.

“These targets, no matter which party is in power, tend to be politically driven. Technocrats are then brought in to justify the numbers,” said Shrestha. He called for rigorous research into how much power Nepal needs domestically, how much it can realistically export, and how much hydropower it should build.



That matters because Nepal’s export market is not guaranteed . India remains its principal buyer and the route to markets like Bangladesh. Yet India has restricted purchases from some Chinese-backed projects in Nepal, and its demand for Nepali electricity is a tiny share of its total consumption.



Kandel argues that energy has always been central to foreign policy and that Nepal should treat hydropower as a strategic asset. “The window is quite limited. Nepal should harness its rivers, without overlooking the disasters, and invest the profits elsewhere,” he said.

But it is unclear whether expanding generation would best serve Nepalis. Each megawatt of capacity costs around Rs. 240 million to build, while weak transmission continues to limit the reliable supply at home.

“Nepal’s electricity must benefit its people. Investment has to shift from supply to building transmission lines and keeping it affordable,” said Thapa.

Nepal depends on hydropower for over 95 percent of its electricity, leaving the grid vulnerable when disasters strike.

Vivek Shastry, a senior research associate at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, recommends diversifying with solar and battery storage. “Everywhere in the world, especially with the squeeze in the oil and gas market, countries are considering how to diversify. There are calls for a serious look at how other sources of energy can play a role,” he said.

India’s experience shows that a grid heavy on solar can be volatile, he said, which is why sources need to complement each other, backed by battery storage, so supply does not depend entirely on the seasons. The costs of solar and batteries have fallen and are likely to keep falling, making them increasingly viable in South Asia, he added. “We need to upgrade grids and build more to connect South Asia.”



As Nepal investigates the Rasuwa disaster and weighs the future of hydropower, Majhi is left to reckon with what comes next on his own. Before the floods, one of the things he valued most about his job at Rasuwagadhi was being able to return to his village in Sindhuli every couple of months to see his family. Like millions of Nepalis who have migrated abroad for work, he had spent a decade in Malaysia.



After the floods, he was relieved that his company paid him for the 15 days he had worked that month. “I lost my money and my phone in the floods, because I had kept it safely in our hostel, but I don’t want to complain when so many people have lost their lives,” he said.



Majhi survived, but 812 workers remain unaccounted for in the tunnels.

title: Nepal’s Mandira Lamichhane Dhimal elected fellow of the International Science Council - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s Mandira Lamichhane Dhimal elected fellow of the International Science Council  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepali social scientist Mandira Lamichhane Dhimal has been elected a fellow of the International Science Council (ISC), one of the highest global distinctions in science. She is the first Nepali woman scientist to be elected a fellow of the council and only the second Nepali citizen to receive the distinction.

The honour recognises her outstanding contributions to scientific research, policy engagement and leadership in planetary health, climate change, gender and public health.

The ISC is an international non-profit organisation that brings together around 250 scientific bodies worldwide. Established in 2018 through the merger of the International Council for Science and the International Social Science Council, it promotes global scientific cooperation.

The council included Dhimal among its newest Fellows, recognising scientists whose work has significantly advanced science as a global public good. According to the ISC, the Fellowship is the highest distinction awarded by the council. It brings together a global network of leading scientists committed to strengthening international scientific cooperation and promoting the role of science in society.

Dhimal currently serves as research director and fellow at the Planetary Health Research Centre (PHRC) in Kathmandu. She is also a member of the Global Young Academy and has made important contributions to evidence-based policy development, climate and environmental health research, and gender-responsive approaches to sustainable development.

Her election as an ISC Fellow marks a significant achievement not only in her scientific career but also for Nepal’s growing presence in the global scientific community. The recognition is expected to further strengthen Nepal’s contribution to international research collaborations and scientific dialogue on pressing global challenges, including climate change, planetary health and sustainable development.

title: Nepal working on expediting death certs for missing Malaysians - Free Malaysia Today
description: Nepal working on expediting death certs for missing Malaysians  Free Malaysia Today
publisher.title: Free Malaysia Today
full_article:
Fifty-four Malaysians remain unaccounted for in the deadly flash floods and mudslides in Nepal’s Rasuwa district near its border with Tibet on Aug 26. (AFP pic)

PETALING JAYA : The Nepali government is working on speeding up the issuance of death certificates for Malaysians still missing in the country’s flash floods in August, says foreign minister Mohamad Hasan.

Mohamad said Nepal was seeking to amend its laws, which now require a waiting period of up to three years before death certificates can be issued for people who remain missing after a disaster, to 45 days.

He said he was briefed on the progress of the move by representatives of the Nepali embassy who called on him last week.

“The Nepali government is pursuing the legal amendments and will table them to parliament. Failing that, it will make special arrangements to ensure death certificates can be issued without delay for the 54 Malaysians who remain unreachable,” Bernama quoted him as saying on the sidelines of an event in Melaka today.

He said the death certificates were necessary for the victims’ families to manage their affairs, including matters involving banks and insurance companies.

On Aug 26, flash floods and landslides hit Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the area near its border with Tibet after heavy rain.

At least 1,454 people were killed and 5,285 missing in Nepal. There were also 43 deaths and 519 missing in Tibet.

The next of kin of the 54 missing Malaysians have submitted a structured financial rescue plan to Bank Negara Malaysia, while the Nepali government works on legal changes to expedite their death certificates.

On a separate matter, Mohamad said Malaysia was awaiting a decision by the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) and the National Security Council (MKN) on aid that could be extended to tackle forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, Indonesia.

He said the outcome of the discussions would be brought to the Cabinet for approval, while efforts to extinguish the fires remained challenging because they were burning in remote areas amid thick haze.

“Visibility is below 50m and the air pollutant index in Kalimantan has reached 1,000,” he said, adding that Malaysia would assess the risks before deciding on air support.

title: Cholera’s hidden price tag: households in Nepal and Mozambique pay a heavy economic toll - bioengineer.org
description: Cholera’s hidden price tag: households in Nepal and Mozambique pay a heavy economic toll  bioengineer.org
publisher.title: bioengineer.org
full_article:
Cholera is usually described in the language of epidemiology: an estimated 4 million cases and roughly 143,000 deaths every year, concentrated in the world’s most resource-limited settings. But a new prospective cost-of-illness study, published in BMC Public Health, shifts the lens from case counts to cash flows, asking a deceptively simple question with profound policy implications: what does a single episode of cholera actually cost, and who ends up paying for it? The answer, drawn from hundreds of consecutively enrolled patients in Nepal and Mozambique, reveals two countries where the same disease imposes strikingly different economic burdens, shaped less by biology than by the architecture of healthcare financing and service delivery.

The research was embedded within the Enhanced Cholera Control projects, known as ECHO-N in Nepal and ECHO-M in Mozambique, and led by the International Vaccine Institute with support from the Korea International Cooperation Agency. Rather than reconstructing costs retrospectively from records, the team designed a prospective cost-of-illness study, the gold standard for capturing the full economic footprint of a disease as it unfolds. In Nepal, data were collected from 38 health facilities in the Kathmandu Valley and Kailali District between 2021 and 2024. In Mozambique, the team worked in cholera treatment centers across five provinces during the epidemic period and in Nampula province during the endemic period, spanning 2023 to 2025. All eligible cholera cases meeting country-specific case definitions were consecutively enrolled, a design choice that minimizes selection bias and yields a sample representative of the true patient population presenting for care.

The analytical framework distinguished three cost categories that together define the economic burden of an illness episode. Direct medical costs cover consultations, medications, laboratory tests and hospital stays. Direct non-medical costs capture the often-overlooked expenses of simply getting treated: transportation to facilities, food for patients and caregivers, and accommodation during hospitalization. Indirect costs, the third pillar, quantify lost productivity, the wages forfeited when a patient or caregiver cannot work. Patient interviews captured all three categories, while healthcare provider costs were estimated from facility records in both countries. In Nepal, the researchers applied a hospital-specific revenue-to-cost ratio adjustment, a technical refinement that corrects for the mismatch between what facilities earn through revenue and what their services actually cost to deliver, ensuring provider-side estimates reflect true resource consumption rather than accounting artifacts.

The headline numbers tell a story of two very different epidemics. During epidemic periods, the mean cost per cholera episode was higher in Nepal, at US$113.5 with a 95 percent bootstrapped confidence interval of 93.3 to 133.7, than in Mozambique, where the mean was US$54.1 with a confidence interval of 50.8 to 57.0. Yet the pattern inverted during endemic periods: the mean cost per episode rose to US$72.5 in Mozambique, with a confidence interval of 65.0 to 80.5, while Nepal’s endemic-period mean fell to US$63.6, with a confidence interval of 48.4 to 78.7. The study analyzed 273 cases in Nepal and 252 in Mozambique, and all costs were reported in 2023 US dollars with 95 percent bootstrapped confidence intervals, a non-parametric resampling technique that avoids assumptions about the underlying cost distribution, which is typically right-skewed in cost-of-illness data.

Raw dollar comparisons, however, can mislead when the two economies differ so dramatically in what money can buy. To correct for this, the researchers adjusted the figures for purchasing power parity, converting local costs into international dollars that reflect equivalent purchasing power across countries. After this adjustment, the mean cost per episode was I$346.9 in Nepal and I$155.3 in Mozambique, meaning that once the local cost of goods and services is accounted for, a cholera episode in Nepal consumes more than twice the real resources of one in Mozambique. This PPP adjustment is critical for cross-country comparisons in health economics, because a US$113 episode in a low-income economy can represent a far heavier real burden than the same nominal sum in a wealthier one.

The most consequential finding concerns who bears the financial weight. In Mozambique, every single enrolled patient received government subsidies for cholera treatment, meaning the state absorbed the direct medical costs rather than the households. In Nepal, the picture was radically different: 89.5 percent of enrolled participants reported making out-of-pocket payments for cholera treatment during the endemic period, and out-of-pocket payments accounted for 92.6 to 96.6 percent of total direct medical costs. In practical terms, nearly every rupee spent on cholera care in Nepal came directly from the pockets of already vulnerable families, a financing pattern that health economists associate with catastrophic health expenditure and impoverishment when illness strikes households with limited savings.

The burden relative to income tells the final chapter of this economic story. The proportion of household income represented by cholera-related costs was higher in Mozambique than in Nepal and varied across income groups, meaning that for the poorest families, a single episode of watery diarrhea could consume a meaningful slice of annual earnings. This income-relative framing is essential for understanding the true distributional impact of cholera: the same absolute cost weighs far more heavily on a household living at subsistence level than on one with disposable income, and the variation across income groups signals that cholera functions as a regressive economic shock, punishing the poorest most severely.

The divergence in cost patterns between the two settings reflects differences in healthcare utilization, financing mechanisms and service delivery models rather than differences in the disease itself. Nepal’s higher epidemic-period costs likely mirror longer care pathways, more intensive facility-based treatment and the absence of subsidies, while Mozambique’s government-financed model shields patients from direct medical charges even as indirect and non-medical costs accumulate. These findings argue for context-specific financing strategies: in Nepal, expanding subsidy coverage or risk-pooling mechanisms could prevent cholera from becoming a household financial catastrophe, while in Mozambique, protecting government financing for cholera treatment remains essential to preserve the existing safety net.

Beyond financing, the economics of cholera strengthen the case for prevention. The authors emphasize that these cost estimates support consideration of preventive investments, from oral cholera vaccines to water, sanitation and hygiene infrastructure, as a means of reducing the economic burden before episodes occur. When a single episode costs I$346.9 in purchasing-power-adjusted terms in Nepal, and when cholera generates millions of cases annually worldwide, the aggregate economic toll rivals the clinical one. Cost-of-illness evidence of this kind provides ministries of health and finance with the quantitative ammunition to weigh prevention against treatment, transforming cholera control from a purely public health argument into an economic one that resonates across government departments.

For a disease long measured in cases and deaths, this study adds a third metric that may prove just as persuasive to policymakers: money. By rigorously quantifying the economic burden of cholera from both patient and provider perspectives in two endemic countries, the research demonstrates that the financial footprint of cholera is substantial, unevenly distributed and deeply shaped by national financing choices. As climate change expands the geographic range of cholera and urbanization concentrates vulnerable populations, understanding what each episode costs, and who pays, will become an increasingly urgent question for global health. The answer from Nepal and Mozambique is clear: cholera is not only a clinical emergency but an economic one, and the solutions, whether subsidies in Kathmandu or sustained financing in Maputo, must be tailored to the financing architecture of each setting.

title: India and Nepal need a common front against Himalayan floods - Firstpost

full_article:
Nepal’s ambitious, six-year plan to drain four high-altitude glacial lakes—Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho, and Hongu-2—is born out of sheer urgency. Following a catastrophic flood along the China-Nepal border that left more than 1,450 dead and thousands more missing, Kathmandu is scrambling to mitigate future disasters.

New Delhi cannot afford to view this as a purely domestic Nepali affair. All four targets sit on a 2020 ICIMOD-UNDP high-risk inventory within the Koshi and Gandaki basins, watersheds that feed the Koshi and Gandak rivers sweeping into Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. For India, providing immediate technical support, data sharing, and early warning systems to Nepal is proactive flood defence for its own northern plains.

Advertisement

Advertisement

The geography of transboundary disasters is unsparing. The catastrophic August deluge surged from the Lhende Khola into the Bhote Koshi, then wound through the Trishuli and Narayani rivers before crossing into India as the Gandak to join the Ganga. By the time such glacial bursts reach the lowlands, they lose their vertical momentum.

The primary threat is rarely a sudden wall of water, but rather an acute, destabilising volume surge delivered to rivers already swollen by the monsoon and hemmed in by fragile embankments.

More from Opinion

The precedent for disaster is well-established. Just two years ago, torrential rains forced Nepal to open every gate of the Koshi barrage, triggering flood alerts across 13 districts in Bihar. The 2008 Koshi embankment breach at Kusaha permanently altered the river's course, displacing over 2.3 million people in northern Bihar.

With engineering design studies slated to begin in the fiscal year ending mid-July 2027, Nepal is drawing on past successes. It lowered Tsho Rolpa by 3 meters in 2000 for the first time and replicated the feat at Imja, a decade later. Yet, engineering has its limits.

The current project addresses only four of Nepal's 21 highly dangerous glacial lakes, leaving the exact valley that failed in August completely untouched. Where engineering fails, technology must step in.

Advertisement

Advertisement

When the August collapse occurred, seismic instruments registered the shockwave as a magnitude 5.2 event. Linked to automated alerts, such data can buy downstream communities precious minutes, provided the monitoring systems are properly maintained.

However, technology requires infrastructure and upkeep. Automated monitoring stations, lake-level sensors, and satellite feeds are remarkably inexpensive when measured against the catastrophic cost of a breached levee.

Facing a $5 billion recovery bill, Nepal cannot secure its mountains alone, and India is noticeably absent from the project's current list of financial backers. This is a missed diplomatic and security opportunity. India already possesses world-class satellite arrays, meteorological assets, and a Central Water Commission that tracks these very river systems.

Sharing this existing data costs New Delhi virtually nothing. Furthermore, the broader geopolitical challenge includes Tibet, where many of the region's perilous lakes reside. Currently, critical alerts must traverse a friction-filled path from China to Nepal to India, stifled by a chronic lack of trilateral cooperation.

But the hydro-politics between New Delhi and Kathmandu carry historical baggage. The 1954 Koshi Agreement remains a point of friction in Nepal, and any unilateral Indian offer to plant equipment in Nepali mountains will be viewed with skepticism. India must shift its diplomatic approach considering these sensitivities.

New Delhi should route its cooperation through multilateral bodies like the UN Development Programme and ICIMOD, the Kathmandu-based mountain center where India holds a seat. By ensuring data flows symmetrically and leaving station ownership with Nepal, India can build trust.

Early warning cooperation is a rare geopolitical arena where one nation's gain does not equal another's loss. During the August disaster, the river gauge at Syabrubesi went offline within minutes of the glacial collapse.

A sensor's sudden silence is a loud distress signal, but only if someone downstream is listening. While lowering glacial lakes takes years, transmitting a digital warning takes seconds and costs a fraction of the infrastructure it protects.

India's major rivers begin in foreign peaks; its domestic security is hostage to what happens in those mountains and how fast that information reaches Delhi and Patna. The August flood decimated a vital border trade route on its way south. The next deluge will not pause at the border. The only remaining question is whether India chooses to hear it coming.

title: Nepal seeks legal amendments to expedite death certificates for 54 Malaysians, says Foreign Minister - The Straits Times
description: Nepal seeks legal amendments to expedite death certificates for 54 Malaysians, says Foreign Minister  The Straits Times
publisher.title: The Straits Times
full_article:
MELAKA – The Nepalese government is seeking to amend the country’s laws to expedite the issuance of death certificates for 54 Malaysians who remain uncontactable following floods and landslides that hit the country in August.

Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said Nepal’s existing laws require a waiting period of up to three years before death certificates can be issued for individuals who remain unaccounted for after a disaster.

He said Nepalese Embassy representatives informed him of the matter during a visit to his office last week.

“The Nepalese government is pursuing the legal amendments and will table them to Parliament. Failing that, it will make special arrangements to ensure death certificates can be issued without delay for the 54 Malaysians who remain unreachable,” he told reporters after officiating at the closing ceremony of the 10th National General Conference of the National Solidarity Association for the 2025 session here on Oct 18.

He said the death certificates are necessary for the victims’ families to manage related affairs, including financial and insurance.

On Aug 26, flash floods and landslides hit Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the Nepal-Tibet border area after heavy rain, damaging infrastructure and communications and complicating search-and-rescue operations.

The Foreign Ministry had earlier reported that a Malaysian who could not be contacted after the disaster returned home safely on Oct 2, bringing the number of Malaysians still unaccounted for to 54.

Meanwhile, Mohamad said Malaysia is awaiting a decision by the National Disaster Management Agency and the National Security Council on aid that can be extended to tackle forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan, Indonesia.

He said the outcome of the discussions will be brought to the Cabinet for approval, while efforts to extinguish the fires remain challenging because they are burning in remote areas amid thick haze.

“Visibility is below 50 metres, and the Air Pollutant Index in Kalimantan has reached 1,000,” he said, adding that Malaysia will assess the risks before deciding on air support and will not deploy pilots if conditions endanger their safety.

On the social unrest situation in Italy and France, Mohamad advised Malaysians travelling to the two countries to stay away from demonstrations and areas where rioters are congregating. BERNAMA

title: Growth, Play and Privilege Shape Preschool Thinking Skills in Nepal Study - bioengineer.org
description: Growth, Play and Privilege Shape Preschool Thinking Skills in Nepal Study  bioengineer.org

full_article:
In the classrooms and courtyards of early childhood development centers across Rupandehi District in southern Nepal, researchers have been quietly measuring something invisible: the building blocks of thinking itself. A new cross-sectional study of 401 preschool children aged three to five years, published in BMC Public Health, has mapped how nutrition, psychosocial stimulation, socioeconomic conditions, and family circumstances converge to shape conceptual skill development during a window of childhood that never comes again. The findings, drawn from one of the first studies in Nepal to focus specifically on conceptual skills rather than overall cognitive development, offer a striking portrait of how biology and social environment intertwine in the earliest years of learning.

Conceptual skill development is the foundation on which later learning rests. It encompasses the abilities that allow young children to classify objects, understand quantities, grasp cause and effect, follow sequences, and solve simple problems. These are not abstract academic luxuries; they are the cognitive scaffolding that supports reasoning, language, and eventual school readiness. Developmental scientists have long known that nutrition, stimulation, and family environment influence cognitive outcomes in early childhood, but evidence from low- and middle-income countries has tended to lump these abilities together with broader measures of development. The new study, conducted by Prakash Sharma of Butwal Multiple Campus, Tribhuvan University, as part of his PhD research, zooms in on this specific domain with unusual precision for the region.

The methodology was deliberately comprehensive. Children enrolled in early childhood development centers across Rupandehi District were recruited through a multistage sampling procedure, ensuring that the sample represented the district’s diverse communities rather than a single convenient cluster. Each child’s conceptual skills were assessed using the conceptual skill development component of a standardized Cognitive Development Tool designed for preschool children. Beyond the cognitive testing, the study collected anthropometric measurements, allowing the researchers to calculate height-for-age and weight-for-age z-scores, the standard indicators of chronic and acute nutritional status. Interviewer-administered structured questionnaires captured socio-demographic characteristics, the level of psychosocial stimulation children received at home, and caregivers’ nutritional practices. Observation with standardized tools rounded out the picture of each child’s daily environment.

When the data were subjected to multiple linear regression analysis, a clear hierarchy of influences emerged. The single most robust nutritional finding concerned linear growth: children with higher height-for-age z-scores, a marker of long-term nutritional adequacy, scored significantly better on conceptual skill assessments. This aligns with a substantial body of international evidence linking chronic malnutrition, or stunting, to diminished cognitive development. Height-for-age reflects not just a child’s diet in recent weeks but the cumulative nutritional history of the first years of life, a period during which the brain undergoes its most rapid architectural changes. A child who is well-nourished through this critical period appears, in this dataset, to carry a measurable cognitive advantage into the preschool years.

Psychosocial stimulation proved equally consequential. Children whose caregivers provided richer stimulation, more talking, more play, more responsive interaction, more exposure to books and learning materials, achieved higher conceptual skill scores. This finding speaks to a growing consensus in developmental science that the quantity and quality of caregiver-child interaction is not a soft variable but a hard driver of neurocognitive growth. Responsive caregiving stimulates the developing brain through language exposure, joint attention, and emotionally secure interaction, all of which are thought to support the neural circuits underlying memory, attention, and reasoning. In a district where many families face economic hardship, the finding suggests that stimulation is one of the few powerful developmental levers that costs nothing but time and attention.

The social dimension of the results is perhaps the most sobering. Children from relatively advantaged caste and ethnic groups scored higher on conceptual skill development than children from relatively disadvantaged groups, an association that persisted in the final regression model. Nepal’s caste system has historically shaped access to education, economic opportunity, healthcare, and social capital, and this study provides quantitative evidence that these structural inequalities reach into the cognitive development of preschool children. The finding is not a statement about any group’s inherent abilities; it is a measurement of how social disadvantage, operating through nutrition, stimulation, healthcare access, and family stress, becomes biologically embedded in early childhood. The author explicitly frames this as evidence for interventions that attend to caste-based disadvantage alongside nutrition and caregiving.

Two findings ran in a direction that might surprise readers. Cesarean delivery was associated with lower conceptual skill scores, and so was increasing child age within the three-to-five-year window. The cesarean association, observed in cross-sectional data, cannot establish causation; it may reflect differences in birth circumstances, maternal health, or unmeasured perinatal factors that cluster with delivery mode. The age association is equally intriguing and may reflect cohort composition, sampling patterns, or the possibility that older children in the sample came from backgrounds with fewer developmental resources. The study is careful to note that these are associations, not proven causal effects, and that cross-sectional designs cannot disentangle the direction of influence.

The analysis also demonstrated scientific restraint in an era of overclaimed findings. Associations for nutritional edema, the swelling that signals severe acute malnutrition, and for household economic ranking were unstable across different model specifications. Rather than forcing these variables into the narrative, the author explicitly declined to interpret them as independent effects. This kind of sensitivity analysis, testing whether a finding survives when the model is respecified, is exactly the practice that separates robust evidence from statistical noise. The final model explained 35.3 percent of the variance in conceptual skill development, a substantial proportion for a study of this kind, indicating that the measured nutritional, psychosocial, and social factors capture a meaningful share of what drives conceptual growth, while leaving room for unmeasured influences ranging from genetics to community environment.

The statistical rigor extended to the diagnostics. Supplementary materials include histograms of standardized residuals, normal probability plots, and scatterplots of residuals against predicted values, confirming that the regression model met its underlying assumptions. A Pearson correlation matrix among continuous variables and a sensitivity analysis with categorical predictors entered as dummy variables further tested the stability of the findings. Ethical procedures were equally thorough: the study received approval from the Nepal Health Research Council, written informed consent was obtained from all primary caregivers, permission was granted by the early childhood development centers, and verbal assent was sought from each child before assessment, with hesitant children given time until they were ready to participate willingly.

The practical implications reach far beyond Rupandehi District. The study argues for early childhood development interventions that combine three strands: nutrition improvement to support physical growth, responsive caregiving and psychosocial stimulation to feed the developing mind, and attention to caste-based social disadvantage to level the structural playing field. In a country where nearly one in three children under five is stunted, and where preschool enrollment is expanding rapidly, the message is that cognitive development is not determined by any single factor but by the convergence of biology, interaction, and social structure. For policymakers, the convergence is an opportunity: each strand is a proven target for intervention, and the evidence suggests that acting on all three together, during the narrow window before formal schooling begins, may yield the greatest returns for the next generation of Nepali children.

title: Nepal’s health reforms need a stronger supply chain - The Annapurna Express
description: Nepal’s health reforms need a stronger supply chain  The Annapurna Express

full_article:
By Shyam Lama, Deepak C. Bajracharya

Nepal has committed itself repeatedly to improve public healthcare, but an important question in discussions about health reform is rarely asked: can its public health facilities obtain the medicines, diagnostic supplies and equipment they need, when they need them? No matter how good a piece of policy may be, or how sophisticated an institution may appear, healthcare cannot be delivered without a dependable supply chain. A hospital without medicines, a laboratory without reagents, or a vaccination center without vaccines is a failing system. Administrative restructuring will take care of little.

Recent media reports indicate that the government is considering three major institutional reforms to address the issues: establishing a Centre for Disease Control to strengthen disease surveillance and public-health response; a Food and Drug Administration to regulate medicines, food and medical devices; as well as a National Health Accreditation Authority to assess and certify healthcare institutions. These are worthy goals as the government seeks to reform its health system, but as their mandates and legal arrangements are being discussed, an opportunity should be taken to address another vital function which seems to have been overlooked in the proposed institutional framework: professional health procurement and supply-chain management. Without a reliable mechanism to ensure that essential health commodities are bought efficiently and delivered when and where they are needed, the benefits of these reforms may prove limited.

The government should consider establishing a National Health Procurement and Supply Chain Agency (NHPSCA), with operational autonomy but public accountability, to support all three levels of government. It should not create another bureaucratic layer but bring together fragmented procurement and logistics functions, existing infrastructure and technical expertise to form a coherent system with clear responsibilities and deliverable results. If designed well, such an agency can help bridge the gap between policy commitments and the everyday realities of delivering healthcare in hospitals, primary healthcare centres and other public facilities around the country.

Addressing a critical gap in health reform

Regulation, accreditation and supply management perform different but complementary functions. A food and drug regulator can set and enforce product standards, but cannot ensure that a district hospital gets quality-assured medicines on time, while an accreditation authority can assess whether a hospital meets standards, but cannot replenish empty shelves. These institutions are essential to a functioning health system, but their effectiveness ultimately lies in the availability of the products and equipment required to provide care. Procurement and supply-chain management must therefore be considered a core health-system function, not a routine administrative responsibility.

Public procurement and resource-management challenges in Nepal are long-standing and reports of the Office of the Auditor General have repeatedly highlighted concerns about procurement practices and management of public resources. Individual responsibility should be held where accountability is due, but recurring weaknesses also reveal the need for stronger institutional capacity, professional expertise and continuity. Health procurement is particularly complex and cannot be managed effectively when it is treated as an additional responsibility for officials who may lack training or time to oversee the entire process. A professional system must be able to anticipate demand, assess suppliers, negotiate appropriate contracts, monitor product quality and ensure that deliveries reach their intended destinations.

Procuring health commodities is not just about getting the lowest bidder. Medicines have limited shelf lives with stringent quality requirements, while vaccines depend on reliable cold-chain systems. Diagnostic products require appropriate storage and handling, and medical equipment demands technical evaluation and maintenance. Emergencies can change demand rapidly, and procurement delays can disrupt routine services and hinder public-health programs. A specialized agency would need multidisciplinary expertise in demand forecasting, strategic purchasing, pharmacy, quality assurance, logistics, contract management and information systems. Its success should be measured not just by the value of contracts awarded or the volume of products purchased, but by whether the right products reach health facilities on time and in the required amounts, at a reasonable cost.

The consequences of supply-chain failures extend far beyond government offices. Nepal faces the challenge of protecting households from high out-of-pocket healthcare expenditure, including spending on medicines and medical supplies. When essential products are unavailable at public facilities, patients can be forced to buy them from private pharmacies, incur additional travel and treatment costs or postpone care altogether. For poorer households, such shortages can mean going without treatment or falling into deeper financial hardship. Reliable procurement and distribution are therefore not just matters of administrative efficiency, but also central to equity, access to healthcare and financial protection. A well-functioning supply chain can help ensure that public investment translates into tangible benefits for patients, wherever they are or whatever their ability to pay.

The proposed agency should manage the entire commodity cycle, from demand forecasting and procurement planning to supplier qualification, purchasing, contract oversight, quality assurance, warehousing, inventory management and distribution. It could develop standard product specifications, benchmark prices and establish framework agreements for federal, provincial and local authorities to use, where appropriate. Its responsibility should not be limited to awarding contracts but verifying that goods are delivered to the facilities for which they were intended. A procurement system that records a successful purchase but cannot establish whether the products arrived at a health facility has not fulfilled its purpose.

Digital integration should be an essential part of this approach. Nepal need not build another disconnected technology platform when electronic logistics and health information systems already exist. Instead, procurement, contract, inventory and consumption data should be linked to provide a clearer picture of stock levels, expected deliveries and emerging shortages. Better information would allow managers to identify problems, redistribute available supplies where appropriate and make purchasing decisions based on actual consumption. The true test of digital reform is not the number of reports a system produces, but whether it helps prevent stock-outs, reduce wastage and ensure that healthcare workers have the supplies they need.

Professional autonomy with public accountability

As a federal country, Nepal must build the proposed agency in a way that strengthens coordination without undermining provincial and local responsibilities. Centralizing every purchasing decision and warehouse in Kathmandu would create new bottlenecks and weaken local ownership. A more practical approach would be to centralize technical expertise and aggregate demand where it offers better value, while retaining distribution arrangements and appropriate operational decisions closer to provinces and municipalities. National coordination could help purchasing power, standardization and supplier management, while decentralized implementation would allow the system to respond to local needs and geographical differences.

International experience offers useful lessons. Tamil Nadu’s medical-services corporation in India and Kenya’s medical-supplies authority provide examples of specialized institutions established to improve public-sector health procurement and commodity management. Their experiences could help Nepal assess the institutional arrangements, professional capabilities and accountability mechanisms required, but neither model should be copied wholesale. Nepal must adapt relevant practices to its federal structure, procurement legislation, existing institutions and administrative capacity, with particular attention to reliable supplies in remote and underserved areas.

The legal framework must evolve alongside the institution. Nepal’s Public Procurement Act and Rules should remain the foundation for transparency, competition and responsible use of public funds. However, a legal review could identify whether health-specific provisions are needed for multi-year framework agreements, pooled procurement, supplier prequalification, emergency purchasing, strategic reserves and lifecycle costing. Health commodities require purchasing arrangements that account for quality, continuity of supply, storage requirements and long-term maintenance rather than focusing exclusively on the initial purchase price. Any specialized procedures must increase efficiency without weakening competition, transparency or safeguards against misuse. Greater flexibility should mean better procurement, not less accountability.

Operational autonomy must be matched by robust public oversight. The proposed agency should have a balanced governance structure, with leadership selected through open and competitive processes and staff recruited according to clearly defined professional qualifications. Procurement specialists, pharmacists, logistics professionals, quality-assurance experts and information-system managers should have appropriate career pathways and opportunities for continuing professional development. Performance should be measured using publicly available indicators, including procurement lead times, stock-out rates, supplier reliability, product quality, expiry-related losses and on-time deliveries. These measures will allow government officials, oversight bodies and citizens to evaluate whether the agency is delivering value for public money. Simply transferring existing positions and responsibilities to a new organization would not constitute reform; the real objective must be to build a professional culture focused on service delivery and measurable results.

Development partners have supported Nepal’s procurement of vaccines, medicines and other essential health commodities for decades. Their experience, technical expertise and established systems could be valuable in creating a stronger national institution, but the transition should be planned to avoid disrupting existing services. The government could invite the World Health Organization, UNICEF, the United Nations Population Fund, the World Bank and other interested partners to support a defined program of technical assistance, workforce development, quality systems and digital integration. Such support should strengthen permanent Nepali capacity rather than create another parallel structure. A credible transition plan should also address how the government will finance the agency’s core operations using domestic resources, while maintaining the continuity of essential procurement and distribution.

An opportunity to act now

The establishment of a new agency need not begin with expensive headquarters or a major expansion in administration. A more prudent first step would be to appoint a small, technically competent task force and give it 90 days to map existing procurement functions, staff, warehouses, contracts, budgets and information systems. It should assess the legal implications of reform, clarify responsibilities across the three levels of government, estimate implementation costs and potential savings, and propose a phased transition. The review should distinguish clearly between functions that should remain with ministries and regulators, those that properly belong to provincial and local governments, and those that could be consolidated within the proposed agency. Carefully selected pilot supply chains could then test the model, identify practical constraints and establish measurable benchmarks before wider implementation.

As the government considers the proposed disease-control, regulatory and accreditation institutions, procurement and supply-chain reform should have its place in the same discussion. The objective should not be to create more agencies for their own sake, but to help establish institutions with distinct mandates that work towards a common public-health goal. Regulation can ensure products meet appropriate standards, accreditation can assess the quality of healthcare institutions, and a professional procurement and supply-chain agency can ensure that essential products are available when and where they are needed. These functions are interdependent, and their coordination could make public investment in healthcare more effective.

Ultimately, the success of Nepal’s health reforms will not be judged by the number of new offices established in Kathmandu or the number of policies announced. It will be judged by what happens in health facilities around the country. Are essential medicines available when patients need them? Are medical supplies safe and reliable? Can shortages be anticipated and prevented? Are public resources being used efficiently? For patients and healthcare workers, these are not just procurement questions, but fundamental questions about the quality, accessibility and reliability of healthcare.

Nepal does not need another procurement committee. It needs professional expertise, reliable systems and clear accountability to ensure that the right health products, of the right quality, reach the right place at the right time. The current debate on institutional restructuring offers an important opportunity to make that objective a central part of health reform. Seizing it will help move Nepal closer to a public health system in which policy commitments translate into dependable services, and patients can access the care they need, without avoidable delays or financial hardship.

Shyam Lama has extensive international experience in health procurement, supply-chain management and emergency logistics across Asia and Africa, including Nepal.
